issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-related trigger content is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. Ambulances is coherent for medical trauma, but military topics suggests a very different trauma context and is therefore clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: Revenge/get-even rumination implies an identifiable perpetrator or assailant. That does not fit a child's life-threatening illness trauma, which is not typically organized around interpersonal assault. This creates a cross-node/content mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies is not a clearly coherent trigger for trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness unless the illness was specifically neonatal/perinatal, which is not indicated. In this profile it sits awkwardly alongside the more plausible medical trigger of ambulances.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Physical self-harm used to stop thinking about the event is possible in PTSD, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile: the only triggers are situational reminders, with no corroborating threat, appraisal, or memory items suggesting the kind of overwhelming internal distress usually linked to this strategy. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should connect plausibly back to the listed triggers; this item is poorly matched.

vignette:
Ravi is a 50-year-old animator, married, with a teenage son. Four years ago, his son was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The treatment was brutal—months of chemotherapy, fevers, transfusions, isolation. Ravi spent every night in a plastic recliner beside his son’s bed, the antiseptic stench of the oncology ward seeping into his clothes, his hair, his dreams. He watched needles pierce his child’s skin, watched him vomit until he was hollow, watched the doctors’ faces tighten when the counts dropped dangerously low. The illness eventually went into remission, but the boy still needs quarterly checkups.

Ravi returned home a different man. He had come to believe that the moment he let his guard down, the cancer would return. He would not sleep in his own bed unless his wife lay beside him; if she traveled for work, he stayed up all night, sitting on the couch with the lights on, because sleeping alone meant waking in the dark of that hospital room, the beeping monitors, the nurse’s footsteps. Now, when his wife mentions even a minor procedure—a dental filling, a blood test—his chest tightens and he insists she reschedule. He cannot bear to be in a medical office; the smell of rubbing alcohol or bleach, even a whiff of hand sanitizer in a grocery store, triggers a visceral memory of the day his son coded and the crash team ran past him.

To manage the constant dread, Ravi has developed mental rituals that he tells himself are necessary for survival. He spends hours rehearsing the worst: his son’s relapse, a car accident, a financial collapse, all possible outcomes meticulously simulated in his mind until he feels momentarily prepared. But the simulation never ends—it only deepens. He also finds himself ruminating about revenge, though there is no assailant. He replays conversations with the oncologist who, he is sure, failed to recognize a symptom early enough; he imagines suing the hospital, or confronting a nurse he thought was indifferent. The anger gives him a brittle sense of control, but it leaves him exhausted and irritable.

He seeks reassurance obsessively. Several times a day he asks his wife, “Do you think he’s okay? Are you sure?” She tells him yes, but it never lasts. A week ago, during his son’s routine blood draw, Ravi stood outside the clinic and watched through the glass, too afraid to enter. The antiseptic smell from the door’s crack made him dizzy. That night, he couldn’t shake the image of the needle, and he asked his wife to check their son’s breathing every hour until dawn. She snapped, “I can’t live like this anymore.”

The conflict brought him to a therapist. He works from home as an animator, but lately he cannot concentrate on his character rigging when he is bracing for a catastrophe. His deadlines slip; his producer has noticed. He is terrified that his son will relapse, but he is equally terrified that his marriage will not survive his vigilance. When asked what he hopes for, Ravi says, “To be able to sleep in my own room once—just one night—without the smell of the hospital.”
